title: Great Leaders Share Their Talents and Skills Beyond the Workplace
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership post argues that generosity is central to a leader's own growth, and that the most potent form of generosity is sharing talents and skills rather than money. It makes the move of looking outside the workplace: busy leaders usually offer their abilities only to family, friends, and colleagues, so the piece urges them to mentor or join projects where their skills help strangers. The author frames involvement, not donations or advice, as the real measure of generosity. The post adds that the best leaders spread the habit by encouraging colleagues and giving them time away from work to do likewise. It closes by redefining charity to include a leader's abilities and asks the reader how wealthy they are on that measure.
points: Generosity of talent, not just treasure, is presented as the form of giving that most develops a leader.
Busy leaders who keep their skills inside work and home are not faulted, but they miss a chance to grow by extending themselves.
Hands-on involvement in projects or mentoring, rather than money or advice, is the author's test of real generosity.
The best leaders multiply the effect by encouraging colleagues to volunteer their skills and freeing time for it.
quotes: If, as many philosophers believe, generosity is the key ingredient to becoming your best self, then how a leader gives to others exerts a powerful influence on how they develop and grow.

But for leaders, it is the generosity of sharing their talents and skills with others that creates a chain reaction of expanding and maximizing potential both for themselves and for those on the receiving end.

When leaders apply and share their talents and skills outside of the workplace, their generosity makes others better. It is this idea, making others better, that is the cornerstone of what leadership is all about.

Finding new venues and opportunities to apply their skills to the betterment of others is how leaders give back. For some leaders, this is about serving as a mentor to those outside the workplace. Others get involved with projects, applying their skills in powerful ways to help others build or create. Involvement, not money or advice, reflects the generosity they offer and feel.

Of course, the best leaders don’t stop with themselves. They promote the idea of sharing talents and skills with others, often encouraging colleagues to do so and giving them the time away from work to get involved.
Good leaders expand this idea to include bringing their talents and skills, and not just their financial wealth, to important causes large and small. Leaders become rich when they give of themselves.
